title: Bengaluru Restaurants Set August 15 Deadline to Quit Swiggy and Zomato
excerpt: Restaurant owners in India's tech capital are giving food delivery platforms a month to lower commissions or face a mass delisting, joining a nationwide revolt that has already seen entire towns pull their menus from the duopoly.
body:
• Bengaluru restaurant owners have set August 15 as a deadline to delist from Swiggy and Zomato unless commissions — which have risen from 16% to 25–30% over six years — are reduced.
  • The revolt follows Namakkal, Tamil Nadu, where nearly every restaurant pulled off the platforms on July 1, switching to local delivery service Zaaroz.
  • Rapido's zero-commission platform Ownly, built with the National Restaurant Association of India, has onboarded roughly 20,000 restaurants in Bengaluru and is now integrated into Rapido's main app.
  • Separately, the Karnataka High Court has ordered Zomato, Swiggy, and Zepto to deposit gig worker welfare fees, with a hearing set for August 14.

Bengaluru restaurant owners have drawn a line: lower the commissions by August 15, India's Independence Day, or they walk. The deadline, set by local restaurant associations, marks the latest escalation in a nationwide standoff between India's food industry and the delivery platforms that dominate it.

The symbolism of the date is hard to miss. Restaurateurs framing their fight as a kind of economic independence from what the National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI) has called "digital landlords."

The Math That Broke the Relationship

The numbers behind the revolt are stark. Commissions paid to Swiggy and Zomato have climbed from roughly 16% six years ago to 25–30% today, according to an investigation by Mint. Factor in discounts, marketing costs, and hidden deductions, and restaurants say they lose 40–45% of every order's revenue before it reaches them.

"I showed them I'm not getting any revenue from online sales. It's just a waste of time, waste of material, and waste of manpower."

— Arul Murugan, Secretary, Namakkal Town and Hotel Owners' Association, to Mint

On a ₹300 order, restaurateurs told Mint, roughly ₹75–90 goes to the aggregator as commission, ₹60–90 disappears in discounts, and ₹15–30 covers marketing charges just to stay visible. That leaves the restaurant with ₹90–150 — less than half. For smaller operators, the margins are worse. One Namakkal restaurateur reported doing ₹5,000 in weekly sales on Swiggy and receiving just ₹100 after deductions.

Several restaurateurs also allege that Swiggy and Zomato launch discounts and enable dine-in reservations without their consent. "If you aren't constantly checking and rejecting these emails, the discounts go live automatically," Ashok Singh Bhati, who runs Momos and Chaap in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, told Mint.

Namakkal Drew First Blood

Bengaluru is not acting in isolation. In Namakkal, Tamil Nadu, nearly every restaurant — except centrally managed chains like KFC — pulled their menus from Swiggy and Zomato on July 1. They switched to Zaaroz, a local delivery platform charging a flat ₹1,500 plus GST per month for up to 100 orders.

The transition has been painful. Daily orders across the town halved from 700–800 to around 350–400, according to Mint. But Murugan, who led the breakaway, remains unfazed. "If you're doing ₹1 lakh in orders and only getting back ₹30,000, it's a waste. Doing ₹30,000 and getting back ₹30,000 is more profitable," he said.

When the Namakkal association had met with the platforms to negotiate, they were told lowering commissions in one city would require a nationwide reduction — something neither company was willing to do.

New Challengers and an Industry Pivot

The NRAI, representing over 50,000 eateries, has been pushing its "Order Direct" movement since 2021. That effort now has a concrete vehicle: Rapido's Ownly, a zero-commission food delivery platform the ride-hailing company built in partnership with NRAI. Launched citywide in Bengaluru in March 2026, Ownly has onboarded roughly 20,000 restaurant partners and charges customers a flat ₹30 delivery fee while taking nothing from restaurants.

"There are absolutely no charges to restaurants. There are no commissions, there are no marketing fees, and there are no subscription fees," Vivek Vashishta, head of new initiatives at Rapido, said at an NRAI town hall, as reported by MediaNama. In late July, Rapido integrated Ownly directly into its main app, giving the food service access to Rapido's broader user base.

Meanwhile, the threat extends beyond commissions. The NRAI has opposed Zomato and Swiggy's entry into private-label food delivery through Blinkit Bistro and Swiggy Snacc — 10-minute delivery services that sell the platforms' own food products. "What we are absolutely not okay with is Zomato and Swiggy doing private labelling and selling food by themselves," NRAI president Sagar Daryani told Mint. Restaurants see this as direct competition on the very platforms they depend on, creating what they call an uneven playing field.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad who rely on Swiggy and Zomato to send meals to family or order ahead before visits, the disruption could mean fewer restaurants available on the apps and a push toward unfamiliar direct-ordering channels. The broader shift may also reshape how diaspora-funded cloud kitchens and restaurant investments in Indian cities operate, as the economics of platform dependence are fundamentally questioned.

What's Next

August shapes up as a decisive month. The restaurant deadline lands on the 15th. The gig worker welfare hearing is on the 14th. Rapido's Ownly is scaling aggressively beyond Bengaluru. And a growing number of customers are bypassing the apps entirely — calling restaurants directly and sending a Porter or Rapido rider to pick up the food, often paying less than they would through the aggregators.

"The economics of giving away 25–30% of every order are simply unsustainable for most food businesses — and 2026 is the year that reality is catching up."

— Industry analysis, Medium

Swiggy has maintained that commissions are arrived at through mutual agreement and that the platform provides significant value through customer access and last-mile logistics. Zomato did not respond to Mint's detailed questionnaire for its investigation. Both companies continue to add restaurant partners — Zomato reported 313,000 and Swiggy over 255,000 in recent quarters — but whether those numbers hold past August 15 may depend on whether the industry's math finally forces a reset.

author: Diaspora Desk
